messages.subject: MCDS with covariable in observation or in sample data
parts:
Dear all,

Tis is the first time I participate in the group. Thanks very much for accept me.

I'm triying to do a MCDS to study the effect of the habitat and the elevationin the estimation of abundance of ungulates, and I have some doubts relative to this:

I have the habitat and elevation of each observation, but each time that I incude the habitat (factor covariates with 3 levels) or elevation (non factor covariates) of observation as covariates, and run the analysis, it shows many warning message. I suspect that this is because there are too much information (each observation with value for the habitat and for the elevation covariate).

Should be better to use this covariable as the sample level (for example give the mean elevation and the dominant habitat of the transect as the values for the hole transect), and use this covariates intead the observation covariate? Will these approache give a more precisse estimation

Thanks very much for your attention and sorry by my english

Àngel Such

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] MCDS with covariable in observation or in sample data
parts:
Àngel

Welcome to the Distance sampling list.  I hope you are learning from reading the questions and answers of others.

Recognise that including covariates in your detection function help to explain variation in detectability, rather than variation in abundance.

If your interest is in abundance estimation by habitat and elevation, then you will want to produce multiple abundance estimates (for various combinations of habitat and elevation).  In this case, I would have thought you would have subdivided your study area into, say, elevation bands (0-500m, 500-1000m, 1000-1500m, or whatever elevations are biologically relevant) and perhaps also habitat types within elevation band.  You could then place survey effort into those habitat:elevation strata and proceed to model detectability and produce abundance estimates.

You will struggle to produce elevation-specific abundance estimates if you treat elevation as a continuous variable.

I realise this does not address the warning messages you receive when performing your MCDS analysis, but I suggest trying to address the large questions first, then move down to the more detailed questions.  You can produce quite sensible abundance estimates without using covariates in your detection functions.  Covariates can be helpful, but not necessary.  Is this of use to you?

parts:
Dear Eric, thanks for your answer,

 

I will try this approach

 

Subdividing the study area in different stratum by habitat, elevation band or a combination of them I have two problems:

1- The habitat is not enough homogeneous to assign one habitat (openland, scrubland or forested) to each transect

2- The number of observations by transect is to low to allow calculations

 

Doing these, I think it should be necessary

1- to classify the transect by the dominant habitat of each transect, even that the majority of the observations would be made in the open habitat patch of a transect classified as forested, because they would be more detectable in the openland, and maybe because they will be more abundant also.

2- Estimate the detection function and the cluster size at the global level (all the transect with he same habitat or elevation band), and then use it to estimate at the sample level (transects).

 

Is it right?

 

Thanks very much Àngel

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] MCDS with covariable in observation or in sample data
parts:
Àngel

I am concentrating upon the purpose of your study.  In your first email you said the purpose was to estimate abundance of ungulates by habitat and elevation.  Did you then allocate survey effort in such a manner that you can produce estimates for the areas of interest to you?

Reading your messages, it sounds as if you did not have habitat and elevation in your mind at the time you designed where your transects were placed. 

Estimation at the sample level is awkward because this does not permit inference beyond the transects you surveyed.  I presume you are hoping to make inference to all of the area with habitat of type "A".  In that case, you would need replicate transects in habitat type "A" and variability between replicate transects will tell you something about how variable abundance is within that habitat type.

What I would suggest instead, is as you say, assigning each transect to a 'dominant' habitat (and elevation?) type.  You might then use "Post-stratification" by habitat/elevation type.  The challenge here will be whether these habitat/elevation combination will occur in sufficient numbers for there to be adequate effort in them to make the inferences you wish.

This is why it would have been preferable to lay out your effort incorporating your study objectives, rather than hoping in retrospect the design matches your objectives.
